title: The same problem: concurrency (goroutines vs the event loop vs MVCC)
summary: Twenty buyers, ten items: Go guards the counter with a mutex, TypeScript hides the bug behind an await on one thread, PostgreSQL fixes it with the check inside the UPDATE. Same bug, same cure in all three: make the check and the write one step.

examples.title: Go: parallel goroutines, a mutex around check and write

annotations.note: The mutex sits next to the state it guards, unexported, and only Reserve touches it. Callers can't forget to lock what they can't reach.

The check and the decrement form one critical section. Goroutines run in parallel on several threads and can be preempted almost anywhere, so without the lock two of them could both see left == 1: a data race, which `go run -race` reports (the race detector needs cgo and, except on macOS, a C compiler).
Results travel over a channel instead of a second shared counter: "channels orchestrate, mutexes serialize". The buffer of 20 means no buyer blocks on sending.
wg.Go (Go 1.25) starts each buyer and counts it. Which buyers win changes from run to run; how many never does, which is why the output prints counts only.

examples.title: TypeScript: one thread, and a race across await

annotations.note: No data race is possible here: one thread runs one task at a time. But await ends the synchronous step, all twenty buyers pass the check before the first decrement runs, and stock goes to -10. Nothing failed; nothing warned.

The fix needs no lock: code between two awaits can't be interrupted, so checking and decrementing in the same step is atomic. The cost moves to failure handling: a failed payment must put the item back.

Promise.all starts all twenty at once: concurrency without parallelism. They interleave only at awaits, which is why the output is the same on every run (lesson ts.async.event-loop shows the queue order).

examples.title: PostgreSQL: snapshots for readers, row locks for writers

annotations.note: Both transactions read 1, and neither waits: plain reads take no row locks under MVCC. This is the TS check before the await.

B's UPDATE waits for A's row lock, then runs once A commits. It writes the 0 the application computed from a stale read, so both buyers were told yes for one item: a lost update. The CHECK can't help, because 0 is a valid value.
A has written a new version but not committed. B's read doesn't wait: its snapshot still shows the committed version, 1. Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.

The check is inside the write. B waits for A's lock; after A commits, READ COMMITTED re-evaluates B's WHERE against the new version, finds 0, and B reports UPDATE 0: sold out. In Go, pgx returns that count as tag.RowsAffected().

use_cases: Stock, seats, quotas, coupon redemptions: any "take one if any are left" decision, made in one conditional UPDATE
Go: in-process shared state (caches, counters, connection bookkeeping) under a mutex next to the data, or owned by one goroutine fed by a channel
TS: UI state updated after an await, where a request that started earlier can finish later and overwrite newer data
strengths: Go: real parallelism on every core, with the mutex making the critical section explicit, and a race detector that ships with the standard toolchain (go test -race)
TS: run-to-completion makes every synchronous block atomic, so the fix needs no lock and no data race can corrupt memory
PostgreSQL: readers never wait for writers, and a conditional UPDATE is checked against the latest committed row, across every process and replica of your service
weaknesses: Go: nothing stops you from touching shared state without the lock; the race detector only finds races that happen during the run you test
TS: the race is invisible in the code's shape; moving one await or adding one fetch can turn a correct function into a lost update
PostgreSQL: under the default READ COMMITTED, read-then-write in the application loses updates silently; you have to choose a conditional write, a row lock or a stricter isolation level

pitfalls.title: Shared state without a lock in Go
pitfalls.detail: Called from twenty goroutines, the unguarded version can sell an item twice and is a data race, which the memory model leaves undefined. Run tests with -race.
pitfalls.bad: func (s *Stock) Reserve() bool { if s.left == 0 { return false }; s.left--; return true }
pitfalls.good: func (s *Stock) Reserve() bool { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock(); if s.left == 0 { return false }; s.left--; return true }

pitfalls.title: Locking the check and the write separately
pitfalls.detail: Two methods that each lock (Available, then Take) are each safe and together racy, exactly like a SELECT followed by an UPDATE or a check followed by an await. Make the operation the caller needs one locked method, one synchronous step, one statement.
pitfalls.good: if s.Reserve() { ... } // checks and takes under one lock

pitfalls.title: An in-process lock in a service with several instances
pitfalls.detail: A Go mutex guards one process's memory, and a TS variable one tab's. Two replicas behind a load balancer each keep their own count. Decide in the database: a conditional UPDATE, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or an advisory lock (sql.transactions.row-locks).

pitfalls.title: Holding a transaction open across slow I/O
pitfalls.detail: Awaiting a payment API between BEGIN and COMMIT keeps the row locked and every other buyer waiting. Reserve and commit, call the payment service, then confirm or release the item in a second short transaction.

quiz.q: In the TS racy version, why do all twenty buyers succeed?
options: Two threads ran reserveRacy at the same time
Each buyer awaits after its check, so every check runs before any decrement
quiz.why: One thread runs the code, but await ends each synchronous step; all twenty checks see left === 10 before the first left-- runs.

quiz.q: B's UPDATE ... WHERE ... AND left_qty > 0 waited for A, then reported UPDATE 0. Why?
options: B's snapshot was taken before A's update
After A committed, B re-checked its WHERE against the new row version, where left_qty was 0
The CHECK constraint rejected the row silently
quiz.why: Under READ COMMITTED a blocked UPDATE re-evaluates its condition on the updated row once the other transaction commits; no row matched.

quiz.q: While A had updated 'fixed' but not committed, B ran SELECT left_qty. What happened?
options: B waited for A's commit, then saw 0
quiz.why: MVCC readers take no locks; B's snapshot shows the last committed version.

quiz.q: Your Go service runs as three replicas. Where must "is there an item left?" be decided?
options: In a sync.Mutex in each replica
In the browser, before sending the order
In the database, in the same statement that takes the item
quiz.why: Each replica has its own memory; only the database sees every buyer, and a conditional UPDATE makes the check and the write one step.

body:
## Concept

"Twenty buyers, ten items" is the same problem in all three languages: a check ("is
anything left?") followed by a write ("take one"). If anything can run between the two,
two buyers can pass the check for the last item. Each runtime decides what can run in
between, and that decides what the fix looks like.

- **Go: threads.** Goroutines run in parallel on several OS threads and can be preempted
  at almost any point. Any shared variable written by one goroutine and read by another
  needs synchronization, or it is a data race. The fix is a critical section: the check
  and the write under one mutex, or the state owned by a single goroutine that others
  talk to over a channel.
- **TypeScript: tasks.** One thread runs one task at a time, to completion. Memory can't
  be corrupted, and synchronous code is atomic. But every `await` ends the step, and other
  tasks run before the function continues. The fix is to do the check and the write in
  one synchronous step and await afterwards.
- **PostgreSQL: transactions.** Many sessions run at once, each in its own server
  process, isolated by MVCC: every statement reads a snapshot of committed rows, and
  writers of the same row queue on its lock. The fix is a write that carries its own
  check, `UPDATE ... WHERE left_qty > 0`, which is re-evaluated against the latest
  committed row when it has to wait.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/C++**: Go's model is yours, threads plus locks, with cheaper threads and a
  channel type built in. `sync.Mutex` is `ReentrantLock` without reentrancy and without
  `synchronized`; `defer mu.Unlock()` is a `lock_guard`.
- **Python**: the GIL hides some races in CPython threads (a single bytecode such as a
  list append is atomic); Go has no GIL, so the unguarded version breaks quickly.
  `asyncio` is the TypeScript model exactly: one thread, switches only at `await`.
- **JS/Node**: the TS example is plain JavaScript semantics. Node is the same model on
  the server; parallelism comes from Worker threads or more processes, each with its own
  memory unless you share a `SharedArrayBuffer`.
- **Databases you've used through an ORM**: Hibernate's optimistic locking (`@Version`)
  is the conditional UPDATE in disguise: `UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?`, and zero rows
  updated means someone else won.

## How it works

Where each runtime can interleave two buyers, and what makes a step atomic:

```text
             runs                                   atomic step                   guards for shared state
Go           goroutines on all cores, preempted     code between Lock and Unlock  mutex, channel ownership,
             almost anywhere                                                      sync/atomic
TypeScript   one thread, each task to completion    synchronous code between      nothing within a step; a
                                                    two awaits                    promise chain across awaits
PostgreSQL   one server process per connection,    one statement; a transaction  snapshots for reads, row
             all at once                            with row locks or             locks for writes, isolation
                                                    SERIALIZABLE                  levels
```

The same bug shows up in each column: Go's unguarded `left--`, TypeScript's check
before `await`, SQL's SELECT followed by an UPDATE of a computed value. The same cure
fixes all three: move the check into the atomic step.

## Design notes

A real deployment has all three at once: several browser tabs, several Go processes,
one database. In-process tools (a mutex, a single-threaded loop) protect one process's
memory, so any decision that involves shared business state, such as stock, seats or a
unique booking, belongs in the database, made by one statement or under a row lock. Go
and TypeScript keep their own concurrency tools for their own state: caches, in-flight
requests, UI state.

In SQL, prefer the conditional write: `UPDATE ... WHERE left_qty > 0` and look at the
row count. Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` when the decision needs several reads first, and
REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE with a retry loop when the invariant spans rows
(sql.transactions.serializable). Under REPEATABLE READ, the racy version's second
UPDATE would have failed with SQLSTATE 40001 instead of silently losing an update.

In Go, keep the mutex next to the data, unexported, with methods that lock; pass
ownership through channels when work moves between goroutines. In TypeScript, treat
every `await` as a place where the world changes: re-read what you checked, or do the
check and the change before awaiting.
